problem:
Consider the following differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+y={sec}^{3}⁡x.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be written as

$$
y(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x+g(x),
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants. Which of the following could be the function $g(x)?$

*Hint: Use the variation of parameters method. You may also wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$
worked_solution:
Suppose we have a second-order linear differential equation with linearly independent fundamental solutions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ Then, according to the method of variation of parameters, we can seek a particular solution ${y}_{p}$ using the ansatz

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}(x){y}_{1}(x)+{u}_{2}(x){y}_{2}(x),\end{aligned}
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ satisfy the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=f(x) \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to this system is

$$
{u}_{1}(x)=-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x,\,{u}_{2}(x)=\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x
$$

where $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ is the Wronskian.

First, we note that the forcing term is $f(x)={sec}^{3}⁡x.$

From the given information, we see that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Therefore, the fundamental solutions to the corresponding homogeneous equation are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We can use the method of variation of parameters if these solutions are independent. So, let's first compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{′}-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since the Wronskian is not equal to zero, this confirms that the functions  ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are independent. 

Let's compute ${u}_{1}(x)$ and ${u}_{2}(x):$

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}(x) & =-\int \frac{f(x){y}_{2}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{{sec}^{3}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x{sec}^{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then, we have $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x,$ and our integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}-\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{3}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{sec}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2}(x) & =\int \frac{f(x){y}_{1}(x)}{W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{{sec}^{3}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x{sec}^{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{cos}^{3}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}(x) & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2}{sec}^{2}⁡x)(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2{cos}^{2}⁡x})\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x}+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{-1+2{sin}^{2}⁡x}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{sec}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is the sum of the complementary and particular solutions, and can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x) \\  & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡x+B\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{{\,-\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{sec}⁡x}_{⏟}}_{g(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
g(x)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\operatorname{sec}⁡x.
$$
